analysis.one_liner: Claws back private equity profits from failing health care firms and cuts tax breaks for health care landlords.
analysis.headline: A bill by Senator Warren and four Democratic colleagues to claw back private equity profits when bought-out health care firms fail and patients are harmed has sat untouched in the Senate Finance Committee since February 2026, with no vote and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets private equity firms that buy health care companies. If a purchased hospital, nursing home, or practice then misses paychecks for months, closes, defaults on loans, or goes bankrupt while patients are harmed, the government could take back — and in some cases criminally punish — the profits, fees, and bonuses the private equity side collected during the decade before or after the failure. The recovered money would go to workers' unpaid wages and benefits and to health needs in the hurt community. It also cuts off Medicare and Medicaid payments to health care companies that sell their buildings to real estate investment trusts (REITs, companies that buy property and collect rent), repeals special tax rules those REITs enjoy for health care property, requires large health care owners to report their ownership, debt, and investor payments publicly each year, and orders a government study of profit-driven cost cutting in health care.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients at hospitals, nursing homes, and practices owned by private equity, who are hurt when firms load up the company with debt and strip out profits; health care workers whose unpaid wages and pension shortfalls would be covered first with any clawed-back money; and taxpayers, who currently absorb the cost when stripped health care firms collapse into bankruptcy. The clawback fund is distributed by the Attorney General to employee benefit shortfalls and community health needs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and staff at private-equity-owned health facilities

how_it_helps.text: When a private-equity-acquired health care firm suffers a triggering event — closure, bankruptcy, 90+ days behind on payroll, rent, or loans — federal and state attorneys general can claw back all compensation the investors, executives, and funds collected within the 10 years before or after the event, including management and monitoring fees, dividends, asset-sale profits, and golden parachutes.

Covered parties whose actions contributed to patient death or injury tied to a triggering event face 1 to 6 years in prison, plus a civil penalty of up to five times the clawback amount, with an affirmative defense only if they prove by clear and convincing evidence they could not prevent the harm.
Clawed-back money goes first to cover shortfalls in employee salaries, benefits, and pension funds, and then to serve health care needs of the harmed community.

The bill bans Medicare and Medicaid payments to any health care entity that sells its assets to, or pledges them as loan collateral with, a health care REIT — the structure that lets landlords extract rent from hospitals and nursing homes at federal expense.
It repeals the special federal income tax treatment of 'qualified health care property' for REITs and eliminates the 20% pass-through tax deduction that REIT dividends currently receive.

Hospitals, health systems, physician practices, hospices, dialysis facilities, surgery centers, and their corporate owners must report each year — publicly, on an HHS website — their ownership changes, debt levels, real estate leases and rents, investor fees and dividends, and offshore domiciles, with audits and civil penalties up to $5 million per false or missing report.

The HHS Inspector General must study and report to Congress on profit-driven practices in health care, including upcoding, staffing cuts, insurer denial tactics, and evasion of state corporate-practice-of-medicine laws, and estimate the financial returns to those benefiting.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity firms and their executives and funds, who face clawbacks of a decade's worth of profits, fees, and compensation, criminal exposure, and up to 5x civil penalties; health care REITs and their investors, who lose federal health care payment flows, tax rules, and the pass-through deduction; and large health care operators, who bear the cost of detailed annual ownership and financial reporting.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity firms and health care REITs

drawbacks.text: The criminal penalty (1-6 years imprisonment) attaches to covered parties whose 'actions contributed' to a triggering event involving patient death or injury, even without proof they intended or directly caused the harm; the only escape is proving by clear and convincing evidence they could not have prevented it, a high bar that could chill legitimate investment in struggling health care facilities.

The clawback reaches all compensation received within 10 years before or after a triggering event, which could capture investors and executives who had no role in the decisions that caused the failure, and the 'unjust enrichment' definition turns on broad conditions such as the firm's interest coverage exceeding 100% at the time compensation was issued.

Cutting Medicare and Medicaid payments to any facility that sells property to or borrows against a REIT is blunt: many hospitals and nursing homes deliberately lease or finance through REITs to raise capital for operations and upgrades, and losing federal payment could push fragile facilities toward closure instead of protecting them.

The annual ownership, debt, and rent reporting requirement falls on thousands of hospital systems, physician practices, hospices, and dialysis providers, imposing a real compliance cost even though the information would otherwise be scattered or private.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — taking back investor profits when a health care firm is stripped and fails while patients are harmed, and using the money to pay workers and serve the community — responds to a real and documented pattern of private equity acquisitions followed by bankruptcies in nursing homes and hospitals. But the bill as written is sweeping: 10-year clawbacks of all compensation, criminal liability with a heavy affirmative-defense burden, and a full payment ban on REIT relationships could overreach, punishing investors who did not cause the harm and starving some facilities of the capital structure they use to stay open. A more tailored version could target the abusive fee and dividend practices without the breadth of the payment ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no Republican support; the Congress is still in session, so it is not yet dead.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on February 11, 2026, joined by four Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — since the referral.
All five supporters are Senate Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats and chair every committee, including Finance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, private equity firms and health care REITs are better off so far: the clawback, criminal, and tax provisions have cost them nothing, and the current rules that let investors extract fees and rent from federally funded health care facilities remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity firms and health care REITs

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors are Senate Democrats; no Republican supports the bill, and Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats and control the Finance Committee.

industries.note: The bill would let prosecutors and state attorneys general claw back up to a decade of fees, dividends, and compensation when a health care firm the fund bought misses payroll, defaults, or goes bankrupt, with prison time and penalties up to 5x if patient harm results. Private equity's returns in health care often come from the very fee and debt practices the bill targets, and those costs show up as staff cuts and closed facilities that fall on patients and workers.

industries.industry: Health care REITs (real estate investment trusts)
industries.note: Health care entities could no longer sell buildings to or pledge assets as collateral with a REIT and keep Medicare/Medicaid payments, and REITs would lose the special tax treatment for health care property and the 20% pass-through deduction on their dividends. These REITs profit by collecting rent from hospitals and nursing homes funded in large part by federal health dollars, a cost that ultimately runs through patients and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Large health care operators and corporate owners
industries.note: They face a new annual public reporting duty covering ownership, debt, rents, and investor payments, with audits and up to $5 million penalties for false or missing reports. They gain nothing directly, but the transparency would expose the financial structure behind consolidated health care, which proponents argue protects patients.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and behavioral health facilities owned by private funds
industries.note: These are among the most frequent private equity acquisitions and the 'specified entities' covered by the reporting and clawback provisions. For-profit nursing home chains have repeatedly gone through bankruptcy after leveraged buyouts, leaving residents and staff to absorb the fallout.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action two months after introduction, no Republican cosponsor, and a Republican-controlled Finance Committee, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or vote on its own; realistically it would only move if attached to a larger package or if private equity in health care becomes a major political issue in the 2026 campaigns. Otherwise it will probably expire with the 119th Congress in January 2027.
